planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; baldhip rose is one of the few native roses that thrives in woodland shade rather than full sun.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; baldhip rose is one of the few native roses that thrives in woodland shade rather than full sun. Small, delicate, single pink flowers open in late spring on slender, sparsely thorned canes with fine, fern-like compound leaves, followed by small orange-red rose hips that characteristically drop their sepals early, leaving a smooth, 'bald' hip that gives the species its common name. Native to coniferous forest understories along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to California, it is unusual among wild roses for genuinely thriving in shade, making it a valuable native shrub for a woodland garden where sun-loving roses would fail to flower. It needs little care beyond occasional thinning of old canes and provides good wildlife cover and berries for birds through fall and winter.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dakota prairie rose is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, well adapted to harsh northern plains conditions.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dakota prairie rose is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, well adapted to harsh northern plains conditions. Fragrant, single pink flowers cover this low, suckering native shrub in early summer, followed by bright red hips that persist through winter as valuable food for birds and wildlife on the harsh, wind-swept northern Great Plains where it grows natively. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, it spreads slowly by root suckers into loose colonies that help stabilize prairie soil, making it a valuable, low-maintenance native shrub for a prairie restoration or naturalistic planting in cold, dry climates where more tender roses would not survive winter. It needs no fertilizer, spraying, or winter protection, dying back partially in severe cold and resprouting reliably each spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; leafy rose spreads by suckers into a low, dense colony and tolerates heat and humidity better than many species roses.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; leafy rose spreads by suckers into a low, dense colony and tolerates heat and humidity better than many species roses. Glossy, narrow, finely divided leaves cover a low, dense, suckering native shrub topped with fragrant, single, deep pink flowers through much of summer, an unusually long bloom season for a species rose, followed by small red hips valued by birds. Native to prairies, open woods, and stream banks of Texas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas, it tolerates the heat and humidity of the southern plains and Gulf South better than many other North American species roses, spreading slowly by root suckers into a dense, weed-suppressing colony useful for a bank or naturalistic planting. It needs no spraying or winter protection and thrives with minimal care once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; chestnut rose is unusually disease-resistant and tolerates heat and humidity well compared to many old garden rose species.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; chestnut rose is unusually disease-resistant and tolerates heat and humidity well compared to many old garden rose species. Fine, ferny, glossy foliage and attractive, peeling, cinnamon-colored bark give this Chinese species rose year-round ornamental appeal beyond its clear pink, single to semi-double summer flowers, which are followed by distinctive, spiny, chestnut-bur-like orange-red hips that give the species both its common name and a striking, unusual fall and winter feature unlike the smooth hips of most roses. Notably resistant to black spot and other common rose diseases that plague many garden roses in humid climates, it is an easy, low-spray option for a Gulf South or humid-climate garden where disease pressure on roses is often severe. The edible, vitamin-C-rich hips are also used in some regions for jams, jellies, and traditional preparations. Prune minimally, mainly to remove old or damaged canes, since it flowers on both old and new wood.
